newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary outlook mixed despite good MOL data. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Hungary outlook mixed despite good MOL data. [CORRECTED 15:40 GMT]

text.p: Hungarian oil and gas company MOL posted results above market expectations, but analysts painted a mixed picture for companies in the domestic market in 1997.

MOL reported last week 1996 net income of 22.2 billion forints ($127.2 million), up from 1.1 billion in 1995. "MOL's results well exceeded consensus expectations," said Rudi Voros, analyst at ICE Securities in London.
(Corrects to clarify MOL reported results last week).
Budapest-listed companies have now completed releasing their preliminary 1996 results and most others were broadly in line with analysts' expectations.

Analysts generally agreed 1996 brought success for Hungary's export-orientated companies, while those more reliant on the domestic market were hit by declining real wages and lower consumption. But they were mixed on prospects for 1997.

James Oates, director for central and eastern Europe at UBS in London, said he expected domestic-oriented stocks such as MOL, tile manufacturer Zalakeramia and telecommunications company Matav to outperform the market this year, he said.
Matav is a candidate for later bourse listing.

"Those which have a strong export component are going to face a much tougher time," said Oates. "One thing I think we'll see is that the value of the forint is going to rise in real terms and that makes life more difficult for exporters."
But Voros had a different opinion about the outlook for 1997. "The economy will grow but I don't think this will significantly influence consumption," he said.
"Companies will grow, primarily the exporters, and the GDP (Gross Domestic Product) will also grow, but firms which focus on the Hungarian market will still face some problems."
The 1996 operating profit of MOL, the highest capitalised stock on the Hungarian bourse, was bolstered by a 5.3 billion forint extraordinary environmental item, Voros said.
"The gas business turned around...and that's the key value driver in the company," Oates said. "I think, overall, MOL was clearly a good performer."
Whereas MOL's 1996 performance exceeded forecasts, chemicals maker TVK and pharmaceuticals firm Egis were below the expectations of Voros.

TVK reported 1996 net income of 7.76 billion forints, according to Hungarian accounting standards, against 10.45 billion forints in 1995. It was hit by the chemicals cycle which fell from its 1995 peak, lowering 1996 foreign currency prices for its main products.
TVK also said the average price of its main raw material, benzene, rose 21 percent in 1996. The result triggered a 16 percent price fall in TVK shares on the day of publication.

Egis, majority owned by Servier SA of France, reported an after-tax profit of 5.58 billion forints according to Hungarian standards in 1996 against 4.90 billion in 1995. Its operating profit rose to 4.97 billion forints in 1996 from 4.03 billion in 1995.

"Egis's performance remained below our forecast," Voros said. "However, our view on Egis's future is positive because a rise in exports can be expected via Medimpex in the CIS countries and via Servier (in western Europe)."
Medimpex is a pharmaceuticals trading company owned by Egis.

Pharmaceuticals company Richter reported its operating profit rose to 9.07 billion forints in 1996, according to international accounting standards, from 5.72 billion in 1995. Its net profit rose to 11.35 billion forints from 7.89 billion.
"Richter proved that without a strategic partner it could rise more substantially than Egis but this (growth) is already factored in its price," Voros said.
Others viewed pharmaceuticals in a different way.
Following the release of the results CS First Boston said it maintained a 'buy' recommendation on Egis, whereas ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett recommended a 'sell'.

As far as Richter was concerned CSFB said it maintained a 'hold', while it downgraded TVK to 'hold' from 'buy'. Analysts said MOL's outlook for 1997 and 1998 seemed difficult to predict as there were a number of questions to be answered.
"MOL's profitability will depend primarily on the gas business," Voros said, referring to the forthcoming quarterly review of gas prices by the government.
Adding to the uncertainty was the planned next phase in MOL's selloff, which is keeping the market on its toes as it awaits details of timing, pricing and offer size.
"MOL's share prices are depressed because new shares will come to the market -- that's why its price did not jump up (after the release of the figures)," Voros said. ($ = 174.5 Hungarian Forints)
